claims.text: Commercial ZrB2 powder can be refined to submicrometer particle sizes by mechanical milling or chemical synthesis.
Field-assisted flash sintering of submicron ZrB2 at about 1600 °C for a few minutes can achieve greater than 98% theoretical density.
The proposed 1600 °C process will produce a fine-grained ZrB2 body with minimal residual porosity.
The proposed process will retain single-phase ZrB2.
Moderate pressure of approximately 50 MPa and applied DC current will generate localized Joule heating during sintering.
The applied electric field and associated thermal gradients will accelerate local mass transport and densification of submicron ZrB2.
Submicron ZrB2 powder has increased surface free energy and greater availability of short diffusion paths.
Rapid field-assisted densification will limit grain growth.
An inert or slightly evacuated atmosphere will limit oxidation during processing.
Monolithic ZrB2 generally requires sintering temperatures above 1700 °C.
The proposed material will have greater fracture strength than higher-temperature single-phase ZrB2 and prior doping-based specimens.
The proposed material will have improved abrasion resistance.
The proposed material will form more stable oxide scales during high-temperature exposure than the comparison materials.
The proposed material will show reduced molten plating-metal infiltration and improved liquid-metal corrosion resistance.
Prior doping-based or traditional lower-temperature ZrB2 approaches have suboptimal oxidation and plating-metal corrosion resistance.
Porosity and oxide inclusions can significantly affect the hardness and oxidation resistance of diboride specimens, including ZrB2 benchmarks.
Excessive dwell time can produce a coarse microstructure and compromise material performance.
Lower-temperature flash sintering will reduce manufacturing cost.
Long-term behavior under prolonged molten-metal exposure and cyclic oxidation remains uncertain until extended testing is performed.

contradictions.description: The method is described as single-step, but it requires a separate powder-refinement or nanopowder-synthesis operation followed by field-assisted sintering.

The experiment specifies identical powder purity and size distributions between batches, while one batch uses refined submicron feedstock and the comparator may be doping-based; doping changes composition and generally precludes identical purity/composition.
